content: The enzyme beta-hexosaminidase subunit beta, encoded by the HEXB gene in humans, plays a critical role in lysosomal function. Specifically, Hexosaminidase B, the beta subunit of this enzyme, works in conjunction with the GM2 activator protein to catalyze the degradation of GM2 ganglioside and other molecules containing terminal N-acetylhexosamines. Beta-hexosaminidase is a heterodimeric enzyme composed of two subunits, alpha and beta, which are encoded by separate genes. Both the alpha and beta subunits belong to glycosyl hydrolase family 20. Mutations in the genes encoding either the alpha or beta subunits result in the accumulation of GM2 ganglioside within neurons, leading to neurodegenerative disorders collectively referred to as GM2 gangliosidoses. Mutations specifically in the beta subunit gene cause Sandhoff disease, a severe form of GM2 gangliosidosis (type II). The HEXB gene itself consists of 15 exons and spans approximately 35-40 kilobases. The HEXB protein is composed of 556 amino acid residues and has a molecular weight of approximately 63,111 Daltons. Functionally, HEXB is one of the two subunits that form beta-hexosaminidase, an enzyme that acts as a glycosyl hydrolase. It removes beta-linked nonreducing-terminal GalNAc (N-acetylgalactosamine) or GlcNAc (N-acetylglucosamine) residues within the lysosome. A deficiency in HEXB results in a defect in beta-hexosaminidase activity, leading to GM2 gangliosidoses, which are characterized by the pathological accumulation of GM2 ganglioside. Genetic defects in HEXB can cause the accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neural tissues, resulting in two of the three lysosomal storage diseases classified as GM2 gangliosidoses. Among these, Sandhoff disease, caused by defects in the beta subunit, is the most extensively studied. Patients with Sandhoff disease exhibit both neurological and somatic symptoms. Experimental therapeutic approaches, such as gene transduction of HEX subunits, have been investigated in mouse models of Sandhoff disease. Intracerebroventricular administration of modified beta-hexosaminidase B in these models has been shown to restore beta-hexosaminidase activity in the brain and reduce GM2 ganglioside storage in the parenchyma. In terms of molecular interactions, HEXB has been found to interact with HEXA (the alpha subunit) and gangliosides, highlighting its essential role in lysosomal enzymatic activity and substrate processing.
